name: Kiran
definition: Kiran is a composite portrait of a thirty-four-year-old Vokkaliga dairy farmer and milk-route operator living in a village near Doddaballapura taluk, Bengaluru North district. His working life balances the rhythm of his own eight milch cattle with the twice-daily collection run he makes to eighteen other farmers, delivering bulk milk to a Nandini society chilling centre before the morning Bengaluru traffic thickens.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Kiran wakes at four-thirty, milks his cows, then loads his small insulated van with cans from neighbouring farms, reaching the Nandini chilling centre by seven. The collection route earns him a margin per litre; his own eight cows bring in roughly twelve thousand rupees a month after fodder and veterinary costs. Afternoons he grazes the herd on common land near the village tank, repairs fencing or bargains for maize and cotton-seed cake at the Doddaballapura mandi. The Devanahalli aerospace park fifteen kilometres away has pushed up land prices and drawn his cousins into construction labour, but Kiran prefers cattle; milk income is steadier than rain-fed ragi, which his father farmed. Evenings he settles accounts with the society, checks his cattle's health and returns home for dinner. Diesel, fodder inflation and veterinary bills squeeze his margin; a sick cow can wipe out two months' profit. He dreams of expanding to twelve animals if he can lease another acre for fodder, but water is uncertain and borewell electricity expensive.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Kiran lives with his wife Kavitha, their two daughters aged eleven and eight, his widowed mother and his younger unmarried brother who works night shifts as a CNC operator in a Hoskote industrial estate. Kavitha manages the household, cooks, cares for Kiran's mother and helps with evening milking; she completed tenth standard and wanted to study further but her family could not afford it. Kiran's elder brother migrated to Bengaluru five years ago, working in a private bus depot, visiting only for festivals. Kiran's father died eight years ago; the family divided the three-acre holding, leaving Kiran with one-and-a-half acres and the cattle shed. His mother receives a widow pension and helps mind the children when Kavitha is busy. Gender roles are traditional: Kiran decides cropping and spending, Kavitha manages the kitchen and children's schooling. Extended family gatherings happen at Ugadi and Deepavali; his wife's parents live in a village near Nelamangala, a half-hour bus ride away.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Kiran studied up to seventh standard in the village Kannada-medium government school, then dropped out to help his father with the herd and ragi harvest; his family needed his labour and saw little point in further schooling for a boy who would farm. His two daughters attend the same government primary school he did, now improved with a midday-meal kitchen and a computer donated by an NGO, though the teacher-student ratio remains stretched. The older girl will move to the high school in Doddaballapura town next year; the Shakti free-bus scheme has made the daily five-kilometre commute affordable, which relieves Kiran and Kavitha. They hope both daughters finish SSLC and perhaps PUC, imagining clerical or anganwadi jobs rather than the dairy life. Kiran regrets his own incomplete schooling but could not have done otherwise then; now he insists the girls attend every day, though harvest and festival seasons sometimes call them home to help. Coaching classes in town cost money the family cannot spare, so the girls rely entirely on school teaching.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Kiran and his family rely on the Doddaballapura taluk government hospital for fevers, injuries and his mother's blood-pressure check-ups; specialist care means a trip to Bengaluru, expensive and time-consuming. His mother's hypertension is managed with subsidised tablets from the hospital pharmacy. Kavitha delivered both daughters at the taluk hospital under a safe-motherhood scheme; the younger birth was complicated, requiring a referral ambulance to Bengaluru's district hospital, which the family remembers as frightening and costly despite Vajpayee Arogyashri coverage. Cattle health worries Kiran as much as his own: lumpy-skin disease swept the area two years ago, killing one of his cows and costing him vaccination and treatment fees he borrowed to cover. Drinking water comes from a borewell; the village hand-pump often runs dry in summer, and tanker water arrives irregularly. The children suffer seasonal coughs and stomach upsets. Kiran's back aches from years of lifting milk cans, but he has never consulted a doctor for it, dismissing it as the price of his work.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Kiran's family belongs to the Vokkaliga community, the dominant caste in the village; most of his milk-route clients are also Vokkaligas, though a few Kuruba and SC households keep one or two cows. The village has a small Anjaneya temple where Kiran offers coconuts on Hanuman Jayanti and during the sowing season, and a Gangamma shrine at the edge of the settlement where women gather for annual festivals. His mother is devout, fasting on Mondays and Saturdays; Kiran himself is less observant but accompanies the family to Melukote for Vairamudi every few years, a pilgrimage his father loved. Community ties are dense: milk collection binds him to eighteen families in daily exchange, and he joins cooperative society meetings, though leadership remains with a few older, larger farmers. Caste hierarchy is implicit rather than loudly asserted, but Dalit households live in a separate lane and draw water from a different borewell. Kiran participates in village temple renovation fund drives and reads Kannada newspapers when he finds time, keeping abreast of Cauvery politics and state elections.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Kiran is a member of the Nandini dairy cooperative society, which means monthly meetings, vote on office-bearers and negotiations over milk-fat pricing; this is his main interface with organised civic life. He holds a Bhoomi land record, digitised, though he once spent two frustrating days at the taluk office correcting an error in his survey number. His daughters receive midday meals and have been enrolled for bicycle schemes; Kavitha uses the Shakti bus pass to visit her parents and accompany the children to Doddaballapura. Kiran applied for a Kisan Credit Card to finance fodder purchases, a process that took six months and three visits to the bank. He has never attended a gram panchayat meeting, though he knows the panchayat president, a wealthier farmer with political party ties. MGNREGA job cards exist in the village but Kiran has never sought such work, viewing it as for the landless. Government veterinary service is free but often the stockman is unavailable, forcing Kiran to pay a private vet. He views officials with a mix of respect, wariness and resignation: necessary, sometimes helpful, often indifferent.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Kiran worries most about water: summer borewells failing, delayed monsoons and the feeling that his village's water table is dropping as Bengaluru's periphery sprawls. He is proud of his dairy herd, the cleanliness of his shed and his reputation for punctual milk delivery, seeing himself as more reliable than farmers who have sold land to real-estate developers and taken factory jobs. He resents the land-price inflation that benefits sellers but raises costs for anyone trying to lease fodder acreage or buy adjoining plots. He blames middlemen and private dairies for undercutting cooperative prices, and believes the government should enforce floor pricing more strictly. Kiran wants his daughters educated so they escape the physical grind he endures, yet he cannot imagine the family without cattle; it is identity as much as income. He views Bengaluru as both opportunity—the city's milk demand sustains his route—and threat: it swallows villages, hires away labour and brings traffic, pollution and water stress. He demands better veterinary services, reliable electricity for borewell pumps and fair milk prices, and wishes his taluk's schools and hospital were as good as those in Bengaluru. He is wary of political promises but hopeful that his vote and his cooperative voice still count for something.
